references.text: In Matthew's parallel account, the young man says the same thing: "I have kept all these. What do I still lack?" ([ref:Matt 19:20|Matthew 19:20]). Matthew adds that the man asks what he still lacks, showing that he feels unease despite his law-keeping.
Mark's parallel account records the same answer from the man: "I have kept all these since my youth" ([ref:Mark 10:20|Mark 10:20]). Mark uses the same expression ἐκ νεότητός μου as Luke.

Paul describes himself as "blameless regarding righteousness under the law" ([ref:Phil 3:6|Philippians 3:6]). This reflects the same attitude expressed by the rich man—a conviction that he has kept the commandments since his youth.

Paul writes about those who have zeal for God, but not according to true knowledge, and who seek to establish their own righteousness ([ref:Rom 10:2-3|Romans 10:2-3]). The rich man's answer shows a similar confidence in his own law-keeping.

"I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life" ([ref:Rom 7:9|Romans 7:9]). Paul's experience contrasts with the rich man's confident claim of having kept all the commandments—a deeper understanding of the law reveals sin.

Moses exhorts Israel: "Only be careful and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget what your eyes have seen… but make it known to your children and grandchildren" ([ref:5 Mos 4:9|Deuteronomy 4:9]). Keeping the commandments from youth was an ideal in Israel, just as the rich man claims to have done.

"How can a young person stay on the path of purity? By living according to your word" ([ref:Sal 119:9|Psalm 119:9]). The psalm expresses the ideal of keeping God's commandments from youth, which is exactly what the rich man claims to have done.
